stances.claim: Every life-threatening escape and chronic illness CJ has survived -- ruptured appendix at 21, dysentery at six, diabetes, heart-rhythm anomalies, hemorrhoid surgeries, the 6x6 army truck -- was attributable to Jesus Christ and his mother Mary, even before he was catechized.
stances.rhetorical_move: testimonial-attribution (retrospective religious reading of secular biography)

stances.claim: Prayer should not be for the removal of evils, devils, defeats, difficulties, and obstacles -- these will always be there -- but for the strength and will to triumph over them, 'in His own way, in His own time.'
stances.rhetorical_move: redirection of petition (asking for capacity, not relief)

stances.claim: Filipino doctors and nurses should practice with both competence (already trained-for) and care -- the second 'C' being the humanity, companionship, and family-presence dimension that depersonalized US hospital care lacks.
stances.rhetorical_move: two-Cs framework with comparative-case illustration (the multibillionaire's US-hospital ordeal)

stances.claim: The Ignatian formulation -- 'pray as though everything depended on God; work as though everything depended on you' -- synthesizes faith and effort without contradiction.

notable_anecdotes: 1957 ruptured-appendix story: as elected FEU Central Student Organization president CJ had publicly opposed the P6 hospitalization fee -- then was rushed to the FEU Hospital and Dr. Alfonso asked him whether he wanted to pay the full bill or the P6 fee. CJ replied 'Doctor, you win. I withdraw my opposition to the six-peso fee.' The ruptured appendix was found at the rear left, not the usual front right, two weeks old but contained by fat envelopment.
1942 dysentery at age six during WWII: no hospital, no medicine, no doctor, no nurse -- given up for dead but his mother 'refused to surrender' and watched over him until he recovered in her arms.

1949 jeepney accident: peddling newspapers, he jumped from a speeding jeepney, fell flat on the road as a 6x6 army truck rolled over him -- his 'lean and thin body' slid under its axles thanks to the truck's high road clearance.

Born Catholic but neither catechized nor evangelized until FEU, where chaplain Fr. Michael Nolan taught him the Our Father, Hail Mary, Glory Be, and the FEU Prayer -- the FEU Prayer later becoming one source of the 'Centennial Prayer of the Courts' composed in 2001 and still recited in the Supreme Court.

Unnamed Filipino multibillionaire's testimony of US hospital alienation -- visited only at specific hours, treated as 'an object to be studied, operated on, and monitored, not as a human being with emotions of fear, loneliness, and desperation' -- used as illustration of the 'care' deficit.

one_paragraph_summary: Repurposing his recent commencement address at the FEU-Nicanor Reyes Medical Foundation as an Easter-season column, Panganiban walks through five life-threatening episodes -- the 1942 dysentery at age six saved by his mother's vigil during WWII, the 1949 jeepney-jump escape under a 6x6 army truck whose road clearance let his lean body slide under its axles, the 1957 ruptured appendix at the FEU Hospital (where Dr. Ricardo Alfonso had him withdraw, in pain, his student-leader opposition to the P6 hospitalization fee), the 1983 diabetes diagnosis under Dr. Augusto Litonjua, and the heart-rhythm anomalies cleared by Dr. Dante Morales's angiogram. Though born Catholic, he had no catechesis until FEU chaplain Fr. Michael Nolan taught him the Our Father, Hail Mary, Glory Be, and the FEU Prayer -- the FEU Prayer becoming a source of the 2001 'Centennial Prayer of the Courts.' From this, his first advice to the medical graduates is to 'pray and trust God always,' asking not for the removal of evils but for the strength to triumph over them 'in His own way, in His own time.' His second advice is to work with 'two Cs -- competence and care,' illustrated by a deceased Filipino multibillionaire's testimony of dehumanizing US hospital care where he was treated as an object rather than a human being needing the companionship, care, and love of Filipino doctors and nurses. The column closes with the Ignatian synthesis: 'Pray as though everything depended on God; work as though everything depended on you.'
